messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing a psychological case vignette
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

Write a realistic clinical case vignette for a patient with PTSD.
The vignette should read as a cohesive, flowing portrait — not a structured report.
Weave together who this person is, what happened to them, how they experience their
symptoms day to day, how they cope, and what toll this takes on their life and relationships.


Do not use section headers, numbered points, or clinical labels for symptoms.
Write 200–300 words in third person.
Cover: presenting complaints, trauma background, cognitive distortions, avoidance, and maintaining factors.
Avoid excessive jargon - write for a clinical case conference audience.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient presenting with PTSD.
Patient demographics:
- Age: 34
- Gender: Male
- Ethnicity: Middle Eastern
- Relationship Status: Married
- Occupation: Publisher
- Trauma Type: Trauma to a loved one
- Pcl5: 74

He is 34, a Middle Eastern man who has built a careful, organized life as a publisher, the kind of work that depends on deadlines, judgment, and a steady hand. Before the event that changes him, he is proud of how much he can manage at once: manuscripts, staff questions, family obligations, and the ordinary noise of a busy household. He is married, devoted to his wife, and used to being the person others rely on. He describes himself then as calm, practical, and hard to rattle.

The trauma enters his life through someone he loves. He does not experience the event directly in the way people often imagine trauma; instead, it is the terrible knowledge of what happens to a loved one, and the helplessness of being unable to prevent it. When he first learns what has happened, he says his mind does not fully take it in. He is at work when the call comes, and he remembers the office around him continuing as if nothing has changed: phones ringing, someone laughing in the hall, a manuscript open on his desk. He feels as though he is moving through the day from a distance, speaking when spoken to, making decisions mechanically, while inside he is already somewhere else.

In the hours and days that follow, he becomes consumed by images of the loved one at the center of the trauma. His mind returns again and again to the worst details, replaying them with a force that surprises him. He tries to push the images away, but they arrive when he is driving, when he is eating, when he is trying to read an editorial note. He begins to dread quiet moments because that is when his thoughts rush in. At night he lies awake, listening for sounds in the house, checking his phone repeatedly, needing to know that his family is safe and near. Sleep becomes shallow and unreliable. Even when he does fall asleep, he wakes abruptly with a pounding heart, already tense, already bracing.

He says he starts to live as if danger is waiting just beyond the next room. Ordinary events take on a sharpness they did not have before. A delayed text message makes his stomach drop. An unexpected phone call sends him into a panic before he even answers. He becomes hyperaware of exits, traffic, loud noises, and the vulnerability of people he loves. At work he is still competent, but his concentration slips. He rereads the same paragraph five times and cannot remember what he has just seen. He misses details, loses track of conversations, and feels ashamed that tasks once effortless now require so much effort. He is frightened by how easily he startles, by how quickly his body reacts to a door closing or a chair scraping behind him.

He and his wife begin to circle the trauma from different angles. She wants to talk about it, to name what happened and to comfort him. He wants to protect her from the full force of his fear, and so he often says little, then later feels distant and alone even in her presence. He notices himself becoming more irritable, less patient with small problems, and then immediately guilty for the sharpness in his tone. There are moments when he feels numb, almost cut off from feeling anything at all, and then moments when grief and fear hit with such intensity that he has to leave the room. He describes a constant internal conflict: wanting to be present for his family, and at the same time wanting to avoid anything that might bring the event back into focus.

As time passes, he begins to organize his life around avoidance without fully recognizing it. He declines certain conversations, steers clear of places or media that remind him of the event, and keeps himself busy late into the evening so he will not have to sit alone with his thoughts. He is aware that this shrinking of his world is costing him something, but the alternative feels worse. At work, he functions on discipline and habit, though there are days when he feels detached from the projects he once cared about. The books, the pitches, the careful shaping of language still matter to him, but less than they used to. He goes through the motions of his role while carrying an ongoing sense of threat, sorrow, and unresolved shock, as if his life has continued moving forward without fully rejoining him.
